body: Argentina has two main license plates: a black one with a black dot in the middle, and a white one with a blue bar at the top. The black dot is unique to Argentina, but the blue bar is also seen in Brazil.
Argentina features a black Google car in Generation 3 coverage. Within South America, only Argentina, Peru, and Uruguay share this feature.

Round concrete poles with three electricity lines in an alternating pattern are common in Argentina. Doubled-up poles are also a strong clue, though similar poles can occasionally be found in Bolivia.
Wooden poles are common in Argentina, with or without a crossbar. Wooden A-frame poles in South America are unique to Argentina.
Argentina is the only country in the Americas that uses white-and-red chevrons.
Road lines in Argentina are typically dashed white, double yellow, or a combination of both.
Argentinian kilometre markers are white with a black strip at the top showing the road number. RN indicates a national highway (white on map), and RP indicates a provincial highway (green on map).
Yellow and red rectangular reflectors on guardrails are common in Argentina and Uruguay. Uruguayan guardrails can be distinguished by the shape of their supports.
Much of Argentina is flat, treeless, and sparsely populated, giving it a wide-open, desolate feel. This landscape is a good general clue for the country.
Many Argentinian cities have unique and recognizable taxis. Refer to the image for specific designs.
Far western Argentina is mountainous, while eastern Argentina is rarely mountainous.
Red soil is characteristic of the Misiones province. This region can look similar to Brazil, so additional clues are needed for confirmation.
The Chaco and Formosa provinces often feature sandy soil with abundant vegetation, primarily low trees and bushes.
This area is characterized by grasslands with scattered tree plantations.
Small lakes near the road can occasionally be seen in the province of Buenos Aires.
Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.
Flat and barren landscapes are typical of central southern Argentina.
Vegetation consisting of flat grass with few bushes is a strong indicator for Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.
Most of Argentina's tree plantations are in the Entre Rios province. However, they are also found in Uruguay and southern Brazil, so look for other clues.
Beech forests are commonly found in the state of Tierra del Fuego.
The Caranday Wax Palm has short, fan-like leaves and grows in low-density forests. It's most common in Formosa but also found in Chaco, Corrientes, and northern Santa Fe.

The Caranday Palm (Trithrinax Campestris) has compact, fan-like leaves and a trunk covered in dead leaves. It is native to the Sierras de Córdoba and is also found in San Luis and northern mountainous Argentina.
The Butia Yatay Palm has arching, pinnate leaves and often grows at an incline. It is most common in Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar in Entre Rios.
The Macaw Palm has small, thin leaves with a visible spear-shaped top. In the wild, it is most common in Formosa, Chaco, and Misiones.
The Cardón cactus has a candelabra-like appearance with fuzzy, golden-brown spines. It is native to the high-elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta, and Jujuy.
The Toothpick Cactus is a large, tree-like cactus with spines that resemble toothpicks. It's found between Catamarca and Cordoba, and on the border of Chaco, Salta, and Formosa.
Wild sunflowers are often found in Salta, Jujuy, and Tucumán.
The Caldén is a large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches, mainly found in La Pampa. It can be confused with the White Carob tree.
Pampas grass is a defining plant of the Pampas region, recognizable by its long reeds and white, fluffy flowerheads.
Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with other hotspots in Salta and Jujuy.
Fields of sorghum, identifiable by its dark red flowerheads, are most common in Santa Fe, Córdoba, and Buenos Aires.
Cornfields are found throughout northern Argentina but are most common in Córdoba, Buenos Aires, and Santiago del Estero.
Fields of sunflowers are mainly found in southern Chaco, and less commonly in Buenos Aires and southern Córdoba.
Latvian-style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza within Argentina.
In Mendoza, you can find poles with a single insulator attached to the side.
White, vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.
These unique markers can be found on provincial roads in Cordoba.
T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have yellow rectangular signs with a chevron pattern on the bottom and road numbers with arrows above.
Red bricks, similar to those in Bolivia, are found in northwest Argentina, especially in western Jujuy.
A unique architectural style in Mar Del Plata and nearby cities features quartzite stone facades, orange tiled roofs, attached garages, and vault-shaped porches.
The Pink Trumpet Tree can be found in cities in northern Salta, such as Orán, Tartagal, and General Mosconi.
Salt pans in Argentina are typically found in Jujuy. They also exist in Bolivia and Chile, but those areas lack Generation 4 coverage.
These red mountains are unique to the RN68 valley in southern Salta.
These volcanic rocks in Generation 4 coverage are only found on the RP43 south of Antofagasta de la Sierra in northwestern Catamarca.
The western part of RN65 in western Tucumán is a small, dangerous road in the clouds, which can look similar to Bolivia's 'Road of Death'.
Red soil with a barren landscape and mountain ranges can be seen on RN76 in Parque Nacional Talampaya in western La Rioja.
These mountains, which are not as high as those in the far west, are typically found west of Córdoba.
This horse trekker coverage is found in southwestern San Juan. A similar trekker exists on the Chilean side.
Vineyards with mountains to the west and flat land to the east are a strong indicator for the outskirts of Mendoza, Argentina's most recognizable wine region.
Semi-coastal grass hills are seen in southern Buenos Aires, especially northeast of Bahía Blanca.
The Monkey Puzzle Tree can be found in western Neuquen, especially on state road 23. These trees are also found in Chile.
Sunrise coverage with degraded image quality is found on RN40 just south of the Mendoza-Neuquén border. The image quality improves closer to the border.
Sunrise coverage with bad image quality and multiple blurs is found on a short part of RN251 and RN22, west of Río Colorado.
The 'sawdust' car, which has a unique sandy dust on its camera, is found in centre-south Argentina.
Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino in northeastern Chubut is surrounded by rock formations. Sometimes you can see the dam to the west.
Comodoro Rivadavia is built on the slopes of Chenque hill, making the city easily recognizable.
Snow coverage is found on the eastern RP25 in eastern Santa Cruz.
Melting snow is seen on the eastern RN293 close to the Chilean border in southwestern Santa Cruz.
These snowy mountains to the north can only be found in Ushuaia, the southernmost city of Argentina and province capital of Tierra del Fuego.
